analysis.one_liner: Bars airlines from charging fees that exceed what the service actually costs them.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would limit airline fees on checked bags, seat selection, and cancellations, was referred to a House committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Fees Act would have required the Department of Transportation to write rules banning airline fees that are 'unreasonable or disproportional' to what the airline actually spends. It targeted the fees travelers know best: charges for changing or canceling a reservation, checked and carry-on bags, and picking a seat. It also required that families with children 13 and under be seated together at no extra charge. Airlines would have had to justify each fee with real costs, and the rules would be updated every three years.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, especially those who pay ancillary fees: families paying to sit together with young children, travelers checking bags, and anyone who has to change a flight. The bill text spells out the benefit for families with young kids, who would get adjacent seats at no extra charge [S3]. Because fees are a multibillion-dollar revenue stream, curbing them could also push base fares up somewhat, but the net aim is to make the total price of flying track actual costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers paying bag, seat, and change fees

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Department of Transportation to prohibit airline fees for changes, cancellations, baggage, and seat selection that are unreasonable or disproportional to the airline's actual costs, and to set standards for judging what counts as reasonable [S2][S3].

Requires airlines to seat children age 13 or younger next to their accompanying adults at no additional charge to the family or to any other passenger, addressing the common practice of charging families to sit together [S3].
Requires the Transportation Secretary to update the fee standards at least every three years, so rules keep pace with new fee practices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which collect a large share of their profits from these ancillary fees and would have to show each fee matches a real cost or drop it. Some of that cost could shift into base fares for all passengers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Airlines that profit from ancillary fees

drawbacks.text: Requiring the Department of Transportation to judge whether every fee is 'proportional to costs' would create a heavy regulatory task, and reasonable people can disagree on what a fair change fee should be, since a canceled seat is not always resold [S3].

If fees are capped at cost, airlines may recover the difference through higher base fares or reduced services, so some passengers who currently avoid the fees could end up paying more up front. This is a general economic effect of fee caps and is not addressed in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is direct and concrete — families would not pay to sit with their own children, and fees that wildly exceed their costs would be barred — while the cost is an unfamiliar regulatory burden on airlines and some possible shifting of fees into base fares. The bill is a genuine consumer measure, though its cost-proportionality standard would require case-by-case judgment by regulators.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the FAIR Fees Act on December 9, 2021, with 15 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to that committee's Aviation Subcommittee [S5].
The full action history shows no further activity after the subcommittee referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The airlines keep charging bag, seat, and change fees that often exceed their underlying costs, because the bill never received a hearing or vote. Airline passengers keep paying those fees.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Fees Act, directing the Transportation Department to bar airline fees that are unreasonable or disproportional to actual costs.

for.name: 15 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all initial support came from Democrats.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 9, 2021, and never scheduled a markup or reported it to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Aviation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 10, 2021, and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the chambers would have split.

industries.note: Airlines collect billions a year in fees for checked bags, seat selection, and flight changes that the bill would force them to justify against actual costs, directly cutting a major profit stream. Passengers pay these fees on top of base fares, so the industry's interest in keeping them runs against travelers' pocketbooks.
